title: When are we officially recognising that lesson planning is a problem?
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: In a follow-up to his earlier post on training teachers backwards, Emanuele argues that the expectation to plan lessons from scratch is a central engine of teacher burnout and attrition that schools systematically ignore. Drawing on the flood of responses he received, he describes teachers thrown into the deep end without materials or high-quality exemplars, and notes that CPD and senior leaders talk about 'workload in general' rather than naming this specific cause. His corrective move is to distinguish the production of resources from the performance of teaching, arguing that novices should spend their limited time and cognitive capacity rehearsing explanations, cold calls and behaviour scripts rather than building slide decks. He equips teachers with a principle to put to line managers - 'I need to see excellence before I can be expected to make excellence' - supported by analogies to surgeons and pilots. He closes by urging teachers to give unions precise language about lesson-planning load so the issue is not lost inside general workload campaigns.
points: Emanuele names planning from scratch, rather than generic workload, as the specific driver pushing novices to work until 2 a.m. and then leave the profession.
His production-versus-performance distinction reframes what early-career teachers' time should be spent on: rehearsing the craft, not formatting handouts.
He gives novices explicit licence to request ready-to-teach, high-quality lessons, backed by the principle 'I need to see excellence before I can be expected to make excellence.'
The piece turns the argument into advocacy, asking teachers to brief union representatives on the planning burden with specificity so it is not absorbed into general workload talk.
quotes: The first truth, is that far too many experienced and non-experienced teachers were thrown into the deep end. I was shared horror stories (including mine) of being told to plan lessons from scratch with zero support, zero materials, and zero high-quality examples from your mentors or schools.

Despite this problem being loud and clear—a massive engine driving teacher burnout and subsequent attrition—there is literally nothing in place in most schools, apart from a few excellent outliers. The reality is that the planning workload, which can consume a novice teacher’s entire evening and directly lead to them leaving the profession, is barely addressed by most Senior Leadership Teams, experienced mentors, and general CPD offers.

I have rarely, if ever, seen or attended a school meeting or CPD session that squarely identifies the expectation to plan everything from scratch as a primary factor in burnout. Yes, we discuss “workload in general,” and some generic productivity tips are shared, but these are far away from the sad reality of teachers working until 2 a.m. to produce low-quality lessons. The problem is not being faced with the specificity it deserves.

As a teacher, you should not be spending the majority of your time on the production of resources (making a slide deck, formatting a handout). You should be focusing on the performance of teaching (mastering the cold call, perfecting your explanation, rehearsing a behaviour script).

A surgeon doesn’t perform a triple bypass without seeing hundreds of models and shadowing an expert. A pilot doesn’t take off without a proven flight plan. We must give our newest colleagues the high-quality plan (structured around Rosenshine, Explicit Instruction, etc…) so they can focus their limited cognitive load on the basics of running the room.

When you speak to your union representative, be specific. Tell them the problem is not just “workload”; the problem is the expectation for novice teachers to plan full curriculum sequences from scratch, which is a key driver of burnout and attrition.
